claims.text: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr is a high-entropy alloy.
A machine-learning transport model can integrate temperature-dependent ab initio electron–phonon and electron–defect scattering rates with experimental conductivity data.
The proposed model will significantly improve electrical-conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model is applicable from 0 to 200 K to nearly ideal, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr samples.
The proposed model is applicable from 300 to 1200 K to HfNbTaTiZr specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Reduced phonon population at low temperature minimizes electron scattering.
Reduced electron scattering at low temperature produces higher electrical conductivity.
Increasing temperature increases phonon activity and electron scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurities introduce defect scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Enhanced phonon and oxygen-defect scattering reduces electrical conductivity.
Calibration against experimental benchmarks will allow the model to capture temperature- and impurity-dependent scattering quantitatively.
The model's predictions will closely match measured conductivity in both specified temperature regimes.
The model will have lower prediction error than conventional analytical models.
The oxygen-containing specimen will have lower predicted conductivity than the ideal specimen.
Existing analytical conductivity predictions assume perfect, defect-free crystals.
Existing analytical approaches do not account for temperature-induced scattering or oxygen-impurity effects.
Neglecting temperature-induced and oxygen-impurity scattering causes significant discrepancies from measured conductivity.
Extrapolation outside the stated temperature ranges or to substantially different oxygen levels may be unreliable.
A relative prediction error greater than 20% at any benchmark temperature would falsify the proposed model-performance hypothesis.
Available ab initio data and variability in purity and oxygen content create uncertainty in quantitative scattering-rate corrections.
